newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic will not hand over war criminals - US.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic will not hand over war criminals - US.

text.p: A U.S. envoy to former Yugoslavia failed to persuade Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Monday to comply with the Dayton peace accord and hand over indicted war criminals to justice.

"That is one area where we have serious disagreement. We are deeply concerned by the fact that president Milosevic does not feel it is possible to send...indicted war criminals from Serbia to The Hague," Ambassador Robert Gelbard told reporters after meeting Milosevic in Belgrade.
"I certainly expressed the enormous priority that the United States and our allies attach to sending indicted war criminals everywhere," he said.
"It is certainly one of the fundamental criteria with which we will judge our relationship (with Serbia)," he said.

The United States has retained some sanctions against Belgrade pending resolution of the war crime issue, compliance with the Dayton accord and improvement of human rights in Serbia's troubled ethnic Albanian-majority province of Kosovo.
Gelbard's visit to Belgrade comes less than a week before Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is due in the Balkans.
U.S. sources said they believed positive results of his talks in Belgrade could pave the way for her visit to Belgrade but the possibility appeared to have dimmed on Monday.
"Milosevic gave away squat on domestic issues," a diplomatic source close to the talks said, also referring to U.S. demands for further democratisation in the country.
Diplomats have predicted Milosevic would refuse to hand over war crimes suspects before Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections due by the end of the year.

Belgrade refuses to hand over three senior Yugoslav army officers indicted by The Hague tribunal in connection with atrocities in the Croatian town of Vukovar during the six-month Croatian-Serb war in 1991.

Four years since it was set up by the U.N. Security Council, the tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminals, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, who remain at large like the majority of other suspects.

So far only nine have been arrested and sent to The Hague, including Bosnian Croat prison camp commander Zlatko Aleksovski. Croatia handed him over last month only after the United States threatened to block major loans to the country.

Albright has said a priority of the new U.S. initiative to reinvigorate international peace efforts in Bosnia is greater support for the war crimes tribunal, which she plans to visit in The Hague on Wednesday.

Albright has said Washington will bring increased financial and other pressures to bear to encourage parties to the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton peace accords -- including Croatia and Serbia as well as the Bosnian factions -- to comply with their commitments.
Many experts see a deepening crisis in Bosnia.

U.S. officials acknowledge that while the Dayton accord ended the Bosnian war, the peace is not secure with signatories resisting integration, return of refugees and cooperation with the war crimes tribunal.
Gelbard said his talks with Milosevic also focused "at great length" on the need for full compliance with the Dayton agreements and praised his positive role in the peace process.

The U.S. envoy said he and Milosevic also talked about "Kosovo issues related to the need to work for further steps to ensure full democracy and consolidation of democracy, including freedom of expression in the country".
